title: IIT Roorkee Graduate Builds His Own Prosthetic Leg, Targets 2028 Paralympics
excerpt: Amputee engineer Saurav Kumar designed his own prosthetic, co-founded a deep-tech startup, and is swimming for India — with Paralympic gold in his sights.
body:
• Saurav Kumar, an IIT Roorkee engineering physics graduate from Bihar and an amputee, designed and built his own prosthetic leg — then became a para-swimmer representing India.
  • He finished fourth in the 100m butterfly at the 2025 National Para Swimming Championship, can swim 5 km in a single session, and was selected for the World Para Swimming Championship Series in Italy — fully sponsored by IIT Roorkee.
  • His target: gold at the 2028 Paralympics. He also co-founded IRIS Eco-Tech, a deep-tech waste-management startup incubated at IIT Roorkee.
  • What this means for you: Kumar's education was funded through a ₹3.6 lakh loan, scholarships and friends' support — a reminder that India's scholarship and campus-support systems can carry extraordinary talent further than family wealth ever could.

Most engineers design prosthetics for other people. Saurav Kumar designed his for himself. The IIT Roorkee engineering physics graduate from Bihar — an amputee — built his own prosthetic leg as its end-user, is now working on automating it for broader use, and along the way became a para-swimmer representing India, with his sights set on gold at the 2028 Paralympics.

From the campus pool to the world stage

Kumar's swimming credentials are already serious. He placed fourth in the 100m butterfly at the 2025 National Para Swimming Championship in Hyderabad, can swim 5 km in a single training session, and was selected for the World Para Swimming Championship Series in Italy on March 12, 2026 — a trip fully sponsored by IIT Roorkee. The Paralympic target is explicit: not participation, but gold in 2028.

His engineering life runs in parallel. As the prosthetic's own user, Kumar brings an end-user's impatience to the design problem — the fit, the weight, the gait — and is working toward automation that could make better prosthetics accessible beyond elite sport. He also co-founded IRIS Eco-Tech, a deep-tech startup building automated waste segregation, incubated at IIT Roorkee's TIDES incubator.

"You don't need a perfect body to chase your dreams; what you need is belief, determination, and the courage to begin."

— Saurav Kumar

Built on loans, scholarships and stubbornness

The backstory matters. Kumar's education was funded through a ₹3.6 lakh loan, scholarships and friends' support — no family fortune, no safety net. His trophy cabinet already includes IIT Roorkee's Professional Development and Innovation Award 2025, the Hari Krishna Mittal Leadership Award 2025, and the institute's snooker championship. "Saurav's story is not just about medals or achievements, it is about courage, determination, and the will to rise above challenges," IIT Roorkee Director Prof. Kamal Kishore Pant told Bharat Horizon.

IIT Roorkee notes it has more than 150 students with disabilities on campus and is strengthening its support systems — a quiet institutional detail with loud implications, given how rarely Indian campuses are designed for disabled athletes at all. Online Media Cafe's profile traces the full arc from the campus pool to the world championship.

Why the diaspora should know his name

Diaspora audiences are used to two kinds of Indian achievement stories: the tech founder and the cricket star. Kumar is neither and both — a deep-tech founder who also happens to be chasing a Paralympic medal, funded by the scholarship-and-loan machinery that remains the most democratic escalator in Indian education. For NRI families weighing what an Indian engineering education can still produce, and for the disability-rights conversation that the diaspora increasingly funds back home, his is the rare story that advances both.

The 2028 Paralympics are two years away. The prosthetic he is automating could outlast any medal. Either way, Saurav Kumar has already proved the thesis in his own quote: the body was never the limiting factor.
